title: HEPA air purifier can improve brain function in just one month
seoTitle: HEPA air purifier improves brain function in 1 month
subtitle: Home use of HEPA filters increases executive function test speed by about 12% in adults over 40
excerpt: Study indicates adults 40 and older were 12% faster in executive function tasks after a month of using a HEPA air purifier at home.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
A recent study showed that adults aged 40 and older performed approximately 12% faster on an executive function test after using a HEPA air purifier in their homes for one month. The result points to the possibility that improving indoor air quality can positively influence cognitive processes.

How HEPA filters work in the home environment

HEPA (High Efficiency Particulate Air) filters are designed to capture very small particles, including dust, mold spores, and pollutants from outdoor traffic that enter homes. By reducing the concentration of these irritants in the air we breathe, the filter can create a cleaner indoor environment, decreasing continuous exposure to substances that research suggests can affect the brain.

Executive function and its importance

Executive function encompasses skills such as planning, decision-making, attention control, and mental flexibility. Tests measuring this capacity typically evaluate the speed and accuracy with which an individual processes information and solves problems. A 12% gain in response speed indicates a noticeable improvement in cognitive efficiency, especially in an age group where the decline of these functions tends to become more apparent.

Public health implications

The findings suggest that the simple adoption of a HEPA air purifier may represent an accessible strategy to mitigate the harmful effects of traffic-related pollution, which is recognized as a risk factor for brain health. Although the study does not establish definitive causality, it paves the way for further investigations into environmental interventions aimed at preserving cognition throughout life.

In summary, the research indicates that improving indoor air quality can be a practical step to support the mental health of adults aged 40 and older, offering a low-cost, easy-to-implement alternative for those looking to protect their brains from the impacts of urban pollution.

With information from ScienceDaily.
